title: A Single Thought Unborn
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (Excerpt from Master Hanshan’s Dream Journey Collection · Letter to Bao Zhongsu of the Ministry of Rites)

inline.s: (Excerpt from Master Hanshan’s Dream Journey Collection · Letter to Bao Zhongsu of the Ministry of Rites)
[You wrote to tell me that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into the fundamental ground, and you hope to obtain one secret word as a shortcut.]

You wrote that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into the fundamental ground, and you hope I will tell you one secret word to serve as a shortcut to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.

[Fundamental ground] In contrast to the transformation-body that is manifested, the manifesting body itself is called the “fundamental ground.” Here it refers to the fundamental nature — what the Chan school calls the original face.
[Fundamentally, this matter has never been secret or not secret;
it only rests on the single present thought of the person concerned

. Even the device of observing the huatou is employed only as a last resort. One need only see through the fact that the perceiving mind active in daily life is entirely the operation of deluded thoughts; even the most profound and mysterious views are but the shadows of the knowing spirit — all matters of mind, mentation, and consciousness. In short, because one has never understood the point of departing from mind, mentation, and consciousness, every thought one raises falls into the old rut of deluded thought. Therefore the Buddha said: All sentient beings, because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, employ deluded thoughts; and because these thoughts are unreal, they revolve in birth and death. This is what Asvaghosa meant when he said: All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.]

Fundamentally speaking, this matter (illuminating the mind and seeing the nature) has never been secret or not secret; the key is to work on one’s own present thought. Even the device of observing the huatou is employed only as a last resort. One need only see through, with full effort, the fact that the perceiving mind active in daily life is entirely the operation of deluded thoughts; even profound and mysterious views are but shadows of the knowing spirit — all matters of mind, mentation, and consciousness. In short, because one has never understood the point of departing from mind, mentation, and consciousness, every thought one raises falls into the old rut of deluded thought. Therefore, in the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Buddha says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time onward, continue in birth and death because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind, the essence that is pure and luminous by nature (because they do not know to abide in the true mind, this essence pure and luminous by nature), and employ deluded thoughts (and so use deluded thoughts); because these thoughts are unreal, they revolve in birth and death.” This is also what Bodhisattva Asvaghosa says in the Awakening of Faith: “All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.”

[Mind, mentation, and consciousness] “Mind” has the meaning of gathering and arising, and refers to the eighth consciousness (the ālaya consciousness). “Mentation” has the meaning of deliberation, and refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas consciousness). “Consciousness” has the meaning of discrimination, and refers to the sixth consciousness (the mano-vijñāna). [Rut (kē jiù)] An old pattern, a worn groove. [The essence pure and luminous by nature] The wondrously luminous essence whose nature is originally pure. Grammatically, “the essence pure and luminous by nature” is an appositive modifying the noun “true mind.” “Pure by nature”: originally pure in nature, without bondage or defilement. “Luminous essence”: the luminous, wondrous substance. [Revolving in birth and death] This refers to birth and death in sections and birth and death in transformation. [Birth and death in sections] Sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the good and evil karma they have created, have a limited span of life and a body divided into sections; therefore their birth and death is called “birth and death in sections.” Those who have ended birth and death in sections have escaped samsara. [Birth and death in transformation] The sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended birth and death in sections, gradually extinguish deluded thoughts and gradually increase realization in the course of cultivation. This migration between delusion and awakening differs in each period; the shift from an earlier period to a later one is exactly like a single birth and death, and its transformation is wondrous, unfathomable, and inconceivable — hence it is called “birth and death in transformation.” Those who have ended birth and death in transformation perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

[From this we know that the various deluded thoughts of sentient beings in daily life are ultimately only a single deluded thought! This one thought is the very source of the initial arising of delusion; from beginningless time until now, there has only ever been this one thought, and no second. Even mind, mentation, and consciousness all arise from this one thought. Only if, in our present practice, we can see through this one thought, will all deluded thoughts and emotional concerns melt away like ice in that very moment! This is what the Awakening of Faith calls: “The mark of being apart from thought is equal to the realm of empty space.”]

From this we know that the various deluded thoughts of sentient beings in daily life are ultimately only a single deluded thought! This one thought is the very source of the initial arising of delusion; from beginningless time until now, there has only ever been this one thought, and no second. Even mind, mentation, and consciousness always arise from this one thought. Therefore, if in our present practice we can see through this one thought, all deluded thoughts and emotional concerns will vanish like smoke in that very moment! This is what the Awakening of Faith says: “The mark of being apart from thought is equal to the realm of empty space.”

[But because sentient beings only see that the deluded thoughts in the mind are myriad and tangled, so very many, they do not realize that in truth there is only one thought. Since, as things stand, the deluded thoughts are tangled and many, the ancients taught people to raise a huatou as their practice. In the final analysis, even the huatou is a deluded thought; but one uses this single thought of the huatou to block the scattered thoughts and gather them into one. If one exhaustively investigates this one thought and peers deeply into it, peering again and again, one finds it originally has no place of arising — it is fundamentally unborn. If one day one realizes that this one thought is unborn, then the root of emotion accumulated over kalpas is instantly severed, and this is called awakening — it is not that there is some other mystery to awaken to.]

However, because sentient beings only see that the deluded thoughts in the mind are myriad and tangled, so very many, they do not realize that in truth there is only one thought. Since, as things stand, the deluded thoughts are tangled and many, the ancient worthies taught people to raise a huatou as their practice. In the final analysis, even the huatou is a deluded thought; but one uses this single thought of the huatou to block the scattered thoughts and gather them into one. If one exhaustively investigates this one thought and peers deeply into it, peering again and again, one finds it originally has no place of arising — it is fundamentally unborn. If one day one realizes that this one thought is unborn, then the root of emotion accumulated over kalpas is instantly severed, and this is called awakening — it is not that there is some other mystery to awaken to.

[They do not realize that in truth there is only one thought] It is like a monkey in a forest that leaps from tree to tree; jumping here and there, it seems as though there are many monkeys, one in each tree, but in truth there is only this one monkey leaping very fast. Therefore the method of stilling deluded thoughts is to tie this monkey to the tree of right mindfulness, accomplish the return of the myriad thoughts to one, and then let the one return to nothing. [Gather them into one] To practice the return of the myriad thoughts to one.

[Now, old layman, in your practice, the place to exert effort in raising the huatou is simply to exert effort in watching this one thought, investigating it deeply, until suddenly you see that this one thought originally has no place of arising. If you realize that this one thought is unborn, then from then on all thoughts are unborn — this is what the Sixth Patriarch meant by “the mind that arises without abiding.” If you seek the mysterious and profound, then there is abiding!]

I hope that you, old layman, in your present practice, will exert effort in raising the huatou only in watching this one thought, investigating it deeply, until suddenly you see that this one thought originally has no place of arising. If you realize that this one thought is unborn, then from then on all thoughts are unborn — this is what the Sixth Patriarch meant by “the mind that arises without abiding.” If you seek the mysterious and profound, then there is abiding!

[Such a direct and immediate approach is the most powerful; it does not lie in seeking much knowledge and views. Here not a single word is of use. You need only first put down all the deluded thoughts and views in your breast, all at once, until the mind is emptied, free and at ease, without a single thread remaining, and then watch the place where a thought arises and exert effort to investigate it. This is to go straight in with a single blade, allowing no room for weighing the past, calculating the future, or any sort of reckoning. The moment there is any calculation, you are far, far away from it.]

Such a direct and immediate approach is the most powerful; it does not lie in seeking much knowledge and views. In this practice not a single word is of use. You need only first put down all the deluded thoughts and views in your breast, all at once, until the mind is emptied, free and at ease, without a single thread remaining, and then watch the place where a thought arises and exert effort to investigate it. This is to go straight in with a single blade, allowing no room for weighing the past, calculating the future, or any sort of reckoning. The moment there is any calculation, you are far, far away from illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
[Old layman, you have set your mind on this matter — why not try beginning in this way?]
Old layman, you have set your mind on this matter (illuminating the mind and seeing the nature) — why not try beginning in this way?
